data.name: Farakh
data.gender_notes: Farakh is used as a male name in Islamic naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: The name Farakh is derived from two Arabic words: Far (distance) and Rah (contentment). It is said that this name was given to a companion of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) who was contented despite living far from his homeland. The name Farakh carries the meaning “Far (distance) + Rah (contentment)” and is chosen by families in Islamic traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Arabic tradition and is also used in Arabic, Urdu, Persian. Parents who choose Farakh usually hope their child will grow to embody far (distance) + rah (contentment) and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: A name that symbolizes contentment and satisfaction with the divine will.
data.etymology: Farakh belongs to the Arabic linguistic tradition and is used in Islamic naming. Its recorded meaning is “Far (distance) + Rah (contentment).”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Farakh total 9, giving a life-path number of 9. Number 9 is linked with Mars and with the qualities of compassion, idealism and generosity.

In modern times, Farakh has become a popular name across various Muslim cultures, symbolizing the values of gratitude, self-discipline, and contentment.

This name embodies the spirit of immigrants and travelers who leave their familiar surroundings to embark on new journeys, carrying the spirit of their culture and identity with them wherever they go.
data.spiritual_significance: The name Farakh also holds a deep spiritual meaning, as it encourages us to find contentment in God and in our Faith, no matter where we are or what life may bring us. It serves as a reminder that true happiness and peace come from within, and that no matter the distance between us and our loved ones or our homeland, our connection to God and to our spiritual selves remains constant and unchanging. The name Farakh instills a sense of inner peace and contentment, echoing the teachings of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) and the entire Islamic tradition.

Ibn Qutaybah's Al-Maqrizi wa Al-Mansub, volume 2, page 197. Farrah ibn Abi 'Amir Al-Awsi, also known as Farakh, was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad and took part in several battles. He was known for his bravery and was appointed as the governor of Al-Kufa by Umar ibn Al-Khattab.
